utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in this courtroom and those assisting us just outside the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, I would like to remind you that the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony still binds you; that is, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. I further inform you that the Chamber has discussed the time your examination would still take. There's a fair chance that your examination will be concluded at the time when your family arrives. At the same time, much depends on yourself. This is not an invitation not to tell the whole truth, but certainly an invitation to focus on the questions that were put to you. And, again, if Mr. Misetic wants to hear further details, he'll certainly ask you so. First, answer your question in a short manner. Mr. Misetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. May I request you -- something before you proceed. I consider you my counsel. You engaged me. I'm not satisfied the way they portraying of this -- these proceedings last night on television, and I know that you will cooperate with them and give them information. So if you gave them the information which they broadcast last night, then I do not consider you an amicable counsel. What am I talking about? On television -- I do apologise. This will be, indeed, very brief, and I shall try to compensate for the time lost in giving brief answers later. They said that I would be shelling myself constantly and, secondly, that I actually introduced a state of war and was killing my own people. I think that that television was at the level of the 1990s. We would have -- we should have made some headway since that period, and someone should bear the consequences for this. I don't know this was portrayed in this way. We, in Serbia, have initiated proceedings against journalists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, your testimony is public, which means that there's no need to give anyone any kind of information which they can find in full in the public domain. That's one. Second, how journalists interpret your testimony is entirely up to them. Whether the picture given is distorted or not, I have no reasons to believe that Mr. Misetic would be the author of any distorted publications. And looking at him, he -- Mr. Misetic, I take it that it's right, that you're not the one who drafts the comments on the television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I expected. And apart from that, Mr. Mrksic, the freedom of press allows everyone to comment on what is in the public domain. There's -- even if it would be a distorted view, then usually investigating a prosecuting journalist is not a proper answer to comments of press. I'm not saying that never a journalist should be prosecuted for matters he writes, but we are all aware, after many, many years in this Tribunal, that the press sometimes gives a fully accurate picture of what has happened, and sometimes the picture is coloured in one way or another. Mr. Misetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if I could have Exhibit D389 on the screen, please, again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm glad that it wasn't Misetic. Okay, I apologise. I apologise for having any doubts. It was not you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you look on your screen, this is the report that we finished with yesterday by Mr. Knezevic. Now, you'll recall that in this report from the 4th of August, he reports as to the first strike being carried out and what buildings were hit. And yesterday you indicated that this was --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A strike in the sense of shelling, not a strike in the sense of industrial action, lest someone should think that that is what the interpreters are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't think there's any dispute that there were no industrial strikes of workers. Now, yesterday you said this was consistent with information you were receiving in your staff. And if we could then turn to Exhibit D1256, please. Now, did you communicate on the 4th directly with Mr. Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic is a member of the Main Staff. I communicated with him. We were communicating up to about 1300 hours or 1600 hours with the corps commanders. And the corps commanders told me the same thing, that it was strange to them that they were not pounding the front, but were shelling elements in the depth. And I received the same information from the intelligence organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 2 in the English. This is intercepted telephone conversations, General. And if we turn to page 2 in the English, which is still page 1 in the B/C/S, this is Mr. Knezevic speaking at 7.00 a.m. on the 4th with an unknown person. And if you see what he's saying there at 7.00 a.m.: "They pounded the area where the command was, all over the yard. "Q. Did you suffer any losses? "I don't know, I can't tell at the moment."

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're asking me. He was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Over here, we haven't had any, but in the town, probably, yes. Obviously, the focus was on the barracks and Presidential Palace. There were so many hits, I don't know how many missiles were fired. It lasted about 25 to 30 minutes." Now, is that also consistent with what your understanding was of what the focus of the artillery and rocket attack was in the initial barrage?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, this was a special artillery strike, and I'm really interested, as an expert, as a general, how come that they were so precise, because we in the JNA did not have such systems as to be able to hit, with the very first fire, such a tiny target in the middle of town. So it had to have a GPS system; it had to have a target enemy group; it had to have a Howitzer system. Probably you did not discuss these matters with your client. This was so efficient, this was with such precision on target, and it was just a single target -- strike and nothing more. All the other shelling was random shelling all over town. And this was rocket shelling, and are you asking for artillery log-books, and you should be looking for rocket logs. You will not find the artillery logs, because there were just a few times that they opened fire from artillery. And I believe that this was done by the Croatian Defence Council. I doubt that this was done by Croatian forces. And one soldier was killed on that occasion, and all the motor vehicles of the car fleet were destroyed. Actually, their tires were punctured. And we all, as professionals, were amazed, how could they have implemented this, how could they have been so on target, because you know how it goes, over-shooting, under-shooting. But they hit the centre, bull's eye, with the very first barrage of fire. There you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's break this up into two elements. When we're talking -- you said the first strike. Are you talking about the first half an hour --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- of preparation, the artillery preparation, the first barrage?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was as part of the general barrage on the town. One couldn't notice that it was there until one came to the actual spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the time. I'm talking about time now. This initial strike, which you say was very precise and you couldn't understand how precise -- how it is that they could have done it so precisely, is that the initial half an hour, the first half an hour?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not half an hour. It lasted all day and all night. But this was the first strike, the surprise attack, the surprise strike, following which there was random shelling by 107, 128-mm rocket batteries. Most of them were 107-mm. I did not notice that strike. I was in this house where I was quartered, and I was being shelled by multiple rocket-launcher rockets. And when I came to the site, I could see that the Command was under attack, and the operations officer on duty told me that it had started in the morning, and it continued. From my position on the third floor, I was able to observe the entire town. I watched, as an expert, how it was being done, and I was trying to assess how many batteries there were, what kind of ammunition was being used, who could have provided the ammunition for them to be using the VBRs, the multiple rocket-launchers, setting buildings on fire and causing panic among the people. And I hid on my third floor -- in my third-floor apartment, I hid behind a piece of furniture in order not to be hit. I found it very strange that the commander continued - the commander of the operation - to pound artillery with such precision, artillery targets in town. And had he continued, we would not have been able to remain at that command post. That was strange, that's was what I found strange. I did not really investigate it further, but at that moment that's how I felt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you: In addition to the Command, the front-line on the Crvena Zemlja -- in the Crvena Zemlja area, which of your forces were holding that front-line?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were from the Knin Corps, a company or two that could be pulled out from the forward end. There was no attack. This is just to show that there was somebody, these troops who are moving about, but they had nothing -- they didn't have engineering devices, they did not have minefields, they didn't have the necessary fire-power, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did regular police forces of the RSK, meaning the MUP police forces, hold any front-line position on the Dinara?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did, but they held the Unista there. This is the part of the ridge which is the frontier of the Republika Srpska Krajina. I went to see their firing positions up there. These were observation posts, and I could see just the forces coming through Livanjsko Polje and through Grahovsko Polje. They actually also had some artillery fire. I believe that a bus was hit; I'm not sure. I observed it from up there, and I could see that we were in a very precarious position that there could be no serious defence to speak of. I even took the president of the republic up there to observe the position, to see the position that we were in. I took him there by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, let me ask you this: If we could please have Exhibit 65 ter 1D1055, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I, meanwhile, seek some clarification of one of the previous answers. Mr. Mrksic, you said this was so efficient, this was with such precision on target, and it was just a single target strike and nothing more. All the other shelling was random shelling all over town. When referring to the other shelling at random over town, did you refer to the shelling that followed the first surprise strike, or could you explain to me what exactly you meant by the other shelling, apparently opposed to the shelling of your Command? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it wasn't just a single strike on the Command and then they waited to start with some other shelling. It all started at one fowl swoop, but the success of the fire was so precise that it was followed by fire all over town. The rocket batteries, the VBR systematically pounded the town. So when I came from my forward command post, where I was resting, to the command place, I had to actually take advantage of the intermissions between the fire, and there I saw people running out of their flats, half-naked women. The children were crying because they were afraid because of the terrible noise which the rockets were making, the VBR rockets. The children were actually holding their ears with their hands, and the women -- the mothers were asking me, What happened? And I heard that rockets had entered rooms of flats. That was the impression I got. When I arrived, I saw this on the spot, and then they told me when it started, there was this one strike, and then this strike was not repeated. We had to change the tires on the vehicles. We had to remove those vehicles and relocate the Command to the reserve command post. And there, one soldier was killed. He was there guarding the car fleet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First, General, as part of the artillery attack, was the Northern Barracks hit?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just as precise a hit as were those on the Command and on the rail station, and they also tried to hit the presidential building. I don't know about that, because Martic immediately moved in with me, so we didn't go to see later. So these three or four targets which were targeted by cannon and Howitzer shells, which were specially guided, their fire was specially guided and managed and directed, and I heard that such systems only existed in NATO, so that they could have such first strikes effected with such precision without the necessary preparation. That is only possible with such systems. I don't believe that the gentleman had those, the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So if I understand your testimony, you're saying that the Northern Barracks, your Command, and the Presidential Palace were targeted precisely. And let me ask you, did you receive --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this: Did you receive information about some of your soldiers being killed within the Senjak Barracks in the first strike?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall. Probably whoever found themselves there had to have been killed because of that fire. I know only about this soldier outside the Command because I was told that, and I know that later, during the day, a colonel committed suicide because he just couldn't mentally bear all the -- the entire situation, the sounds, because there were some officers there who had never been in battle, who had never felt -- who had never had any war experiences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the Senjak Barracks was also targeted in the first strike?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. The barracks in which UNPROFOR was, was not hit, and I don't know what its name was. I was there for only two months. I hadn't had time to visit all the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you a different way. Colonel Bjelanovic was your logistics officer. Do you know where his base was?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him once, I visited him once. There was some sheds, as far as I remember. He did everything he could prior to the aggression to effect a dispersion through the valley where Milka Planac [phoen] was supposed to have a railway or a tunnel built, so we dispersed the people into those tunnels, and our equipment also. It was only some explosives and equipment that remained in the depots, because I also ordered that they should not be used because there could be damage to the Republika Srpska, and I was thinking that we would be using it later for some purposes that would be of benefit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How would you get and transport the explosives and equipment that remained in the depots? If you needed to transport it up to the Dinara and to the front-line, how would you get it from the tunnels to Dinara?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Excuse me. Let me just -- can we just have clarification about which depots, in particular, we're referring to? I'm asking for clarification on which depots he's referring to, if you can just ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's keep matters a bit --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. You said some explosives and some equipment remained in the depots. A simple question: Where were these depots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The depots were in the Zrmanja Valley. These gentlemen would know, the commanders. These were large depots, and there were some cars -- railway cars in them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let me keep it quite simple. I wasn't asking you about the size of it, but where it was. You've answered that question. You said in the Zrmanja Valley. Were there any depots in Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. These were mobile depots. The army had taken them away with them from the warehouses. Mr. President, when I referred to depots, I mean large army depots, and it would be sufficient -- to activate one such depot, half of Knin would be destroyed as a result in the tremors that would follow. Because we did not proceed to destroy anything, any roads or bridges or anything; we didn't really need the explosives. We only took with us what we needed for combat fighting on the front-line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the next question that Mr. Misetic put to you is: From what depots was equipment transported to your positions at Dinara? What depots? I'm just asking that, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we took only ammunition that any combatant would take with him. We didn't need any explosive there. We didn't have any contact mines, nor any mines that were required for destroying roads or bills [as interpreted], because this was -- these were very high elevations. If the soldier was on foot, he couldn't carry all this with him. And we didn't even go up there or take anything up there, because this wasn't our territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, please listen carefully to Mr. Misetic's next question. He'll put a focused question to you; you give a focused answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, well, first of all, you, in fact, did on the 4th of August receive requests for additional ammunition. And in fact you, yourself, sent a request to Mr. Perisic in Belgrade to send you more ammunition, explosives, et cetera; correct? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. It is possible that the logistics people did request something. However, the replenishment with ammunition happened some 15 days to a month before the aggression, but the -- we only took the ammunition that was in excess of the normal contingents that were paid by the government.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last portion of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you just repeat the last portion of what you said, General.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall now, we had ammunition in Ceketovac [phoen], I believe, near Dvor, in that depot, and in Knin, and also the ammunition that the corps reserves had. So we had ammunition for about a few days of fighting. Whether there was a telegram sent with such requests or not, whether someone sent it, I can't really recall right now. But, you know, when it's tough, then everyone calls for ammunition and requests ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem that we had was artillery ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Registrar, if I could have Exhibit D161, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us, while we're pulling that up, what was in Golubic?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what it's all about. That's the large depot for the former JNA for this entire area between Split and all the way to the Dalmatian Plateau. This was the main depot in Golubici. And there was also a police base in Golubici, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How would you transport that ammunition in Golubic to units, by what means?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ammunition was transported from those depots. I don't know actually what you mean by "ammunition." Do you mean the ammunition that was in depots, in the stationary depots in the hills? That ammunition had been pulled out 15 days before the aggression started. It wasn't even there anymore. What was left there was what we didn't really need anymore; explosives, maybe some anti-tank mines and so on. After all, you know what you found there. And as for ammunition, all of it had been pulled out. Going along the valley towards Srb and then Golubici, there are some tunnels there, so it was possible to use transport vehicles from Republika Srpska to go through there and to bring ammunition that we needed. This is the so-called dispersion. Dispersion is effected as soon as a state of war is declared. That's normal; that's what every army prepares for its defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 5 in the English on this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is Mr. Bjelanovic's diary from the 4th of August --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tiskovac , yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me get the right page in the B/C/S. Page 7 in the B/C/S, please. Now, this is his diary. On the 4th of August, he's your chief logistics officer. He says, in the middle of the first -- he says: "The attack began at 5.00. At 5.30, I was personally at the SVK Main Staff Operative Centre, where together with the corps command, I monitored the situation in the units. The system of logistical support was in function in the SVK units. The first request from units came about 11.00 from the 7th Corps assistant commander for logistics regarding replenishment of artillery ammunition, which was personally approved by the commander on the suggestion of the chief of artillery." We go down a little bit: "At 1125 hours, I gave an order to my deputy to send vehicles of the 75th Logistics Base to the Golubici --"

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, logistics, not infantry. Logistics or rear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm reading the English version.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the translation is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Send the vehicles of the 75th Logistics Base to the Golubici depot to load the 60.82 and 120-millimetre shells. "At 1200 hours, artillery ammunition was issued on request of the 21st Corps Command."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, before we look at that next section, General, based on this, does that refresh your recollection that the ARSK was obtaining what looks like artillery --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. It does, it does refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So you were using vehicles to transport this artillery from Golubic to someplace else; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was the replenishment of the 39 Corps, which was the closest. It was deployed on positions around Golubici, the 39th. And as for the 21st, the Kordun Corps, it did not come for ammunition to Golubici, because they had their own ammunition. They could not touch the ammunition store there without the commander's approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Where would -- the 7th Corps assistant commander for logistics, where would he deploy his artillery ammunition?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he would deploy the units which had expended the ammunition, those units that had actually engaged the enemy. And most of the fighting was on the Dinara slopes. You did not even attack us from below. You just sort of nudged us a little. There were some home guards units down there, I believe, because at this time the commanders were on the front-line, and this is where most of the ammunition was expended. The greatest expenditure of ammunition was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that's my question, is: How did you get that ammunition -- those vehicles, that it says here, were moving ammunition from Golubic to that front-line position of the 7th Corps, how would they get from Golubic to the front-line?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand what you're trying to ask me. Golubic was not targeted. It was just the depot. It was not your intention to shoot or target Golubic. Knin was the target. And they went there to replenish and pull stuff out. They went along the road, and there were some soldiers from Grahovo there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What route -- what communication would you take from Golubic to the positions on the Dinara?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you would take the route up the Dinara Mountain, towards Grahovo. There was no one left on Mount Dinara, if you mean Dinara the mountain. It had already been taken beforehand, before the attack. No one even tried to defend that part. There was only UNPROFOR people who complained that they were fired by mortars, and I had sought permission to actually fire at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's look at this page that's on the screen now. It says: "At 1620, I," and it refers to Mr. Bjelanovic, "went to the rear command post, Senjak Barracks, and had a short meeting with senior officers and deployed them."

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're not reading this correctly. What it says here in Croat-Serbian or Serbo-Croatian, Milanovic was there throughout this time, and if you're reading from 1820, no. Okay 1620, all right. Let me see. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, were you aware of your logistics officer holding a meeting at 1620 in the Senjak barracks, which is the -- I think we all agree is the compound across from the Tvik factory.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the North Barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right, all right, you probably know this better than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm surprised to hear that, General. Are you aware of that there was a military barracks --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have any time to, you know, make tours of the barracks at the time. I told you what I did. I had to resolve some major issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, General, then that leads me -- we can cut this discussion --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just cut --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- this discussion short. If you didn't know there was a barracks across from the Tvik factory, then are you sure that the artillery that was coming in and firing wasn't firing on military objectives, if you didn't have time to go through the town and know where they all were?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the barracks where the corps command was, the Command of the Dalmatia Corps. It was called the North Barracks, I know, and that's where I was. There was also a barrack where there was a base of some sort, and Bjelanovic was there. Then there was another barrack where the UNPROFOR members were stationed. There was the Command. Whether there were some other barracks, whether there were some prisons or something of that sort, I have no idea. Believe me, I did not serve there, really, for long. And even the time that I spent there, I spent more outside of Knin than in Knin itself. And that he did have this meeting, I believe that, yes, Bjelanovic did probably hold this meeting and issue tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We can move on, General. That's fine. If I can turn your attention to 65 ter 1D1055, please. Do you recall General Kovacevic, after Operation Storm, on the 9th of August sending a report to the SVK General Staff about the events in Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was not the only one. Everyone sent reports so that an analysis could be drafted to see what had happened to us, why it had come about, how it could have happened, and so on. So there was this whole study that was actually done in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, if you will --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I would like to know is -- this was probably a document provided by the Serbian government to the Croatian government, and then the Croatian government provided it to you. Well, I don't think it's relevant. Oh, I see, the Prosecutor was the one. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. So if you would, to make it easier for you -- Mr. President, with your permission, I'll give him a hard copy of this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. At the same -- Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I wasn't actually looking, but I heard that he indicates that the Prosecutor gave it to you. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not spend time on matters which appear to be not relevant. Whether the witness has thoughts about where documents originate from is not of major relevance, I would say, unless there's any specific reason to believe that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, the question just was whether you are aware of a report sent by - let me see - it was General Kovacevic, sending a report on the 9th. Mr. Misetic at this moment is not interested whether any other reports were sent, whether reports were sent frequently. He just wants to know whether you have any recollection of this report by General Novakovic that was sent on the 9th of August. Do you have any recollection of that, this specific report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any recollection of this particular report, but I haven't had an opportunity to read it. I don't really know what it's all about, but I see that there is no signature. And the way we did these reports, and this general was the chief of an administration in the General Staff, he wouldn't have provided a document like this. Anyway, I don't recall this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the answer to the question, and all the further comments are, at this moment, not asked from you. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to page -- go to the bottom of the English, which is paragraph 5, and then we'll continue on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But if you could go to numbered paragraph 5, General. Okay. General Kovacevic reports that on 4 August, at 0500 hours, the Ustasha forces commenced the preparations and the offensive operations on the entire front-line of the 7th Corps. The artillery was permanently actively engaged until 2030 hours." If you could turn the page, please. Yes: "Already at around 1000 hours on 4 August, the forces of the police battalion that were holding the positions at the Dinara Mountain started retreating in an organised manner, which resulted in the retreat of the remaining units of the 7th Corps. Although the 7th Corps tried to further retain the positions at the Dinara, due to the weak entrenchment and suppression and the horrible pressure on the unaccustomed soldiers imposed by the Ustasha artillery, the dominant positions were abandoned and only parts of the units occupied in a disorganized manner the unprepared positions in the depth ..." Now, does that refresh your recollection about the role that the police battalion had in holding the position on the Dinara Mountain?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these were the forces that I mentioned earlier that I went -- used the helicopter to go up there to review these forces. I took President Martic there because these were his forces, and I took him there to review these. And this helps remind me that this was an order that I actually -- or this was something that I actually heard from General Novakovic orally. Yes, now you've jogged my memory and reminding me of the problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Going on into paragraphs -- numbered paragraph 6 -- okay, sorry, I apologise. Can we go back up to paragraph 5, paragraph 5. And just in terms of what we were talking about yesterday, General Kovacevic reports in that last sentence in paragraph 5: "At the same time, the Ustasha forces exerted great pressure on the units of the 15th Corps over the Velebit Mountain and captured the Nac Alan, so that there was a threatening danger that in the course of 5 and 6 August, by emerging in Knin and Gracac, the Ustasha would cut off and encircle the 7th Corps, which would have catastrophic consequences."

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's what you said yesterday about Otric --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, exactly, yes. The portion of the forces that I had brought from the Special Corps to Bruvno -- what was the name? Yes, that's what this is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. President, if I could have this exhibit marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1516.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Registrar, if we could have Exhibit D828, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is the report of Commander Uzelac, who was the commander in Benkovac; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, at the bottom of page 1 in the English, there's a paragraph that says: "Around 80 shells were fired on the town of Benkovac ..." Do you see that? It says: "Around 80 shells were fired on the town of Benkovac until 0800 hours, and around 100 shells on the forward line of brigade defences. Our forces did not open fire." If you could turn the page in the English: "We had neither injured nor killed in both town and the unit until 0800 on 4 August 1995." Now, is that information about the shelling of Benkovac consistent with the information you were receiving on the morning of the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I received information from corps commanders, you see. I did not have any contact with brigade commanders. If they informed or reported to their corps commanders, I have no reason to doubt them. But I would like to take a look at this document, because I can only see the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We'll get back to it in a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right, all right, you'll let me read it later. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So as of -- let me just ask you something specific on this. On the morning of the 4th of August, by 8.00 a.m. was your information that although Benkovac had been shelled, that there were no injured or killed in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have the specific information in front of me, but I had information that all towns had been fired upon; Benkovac, Drnis, Vojnic, Vrgin Most, Korenica, Glina. I mean, the operation or the action had started not along the front-line but in depth, and even Vrgin Most, which had been fired at long range, and we were all caught by surprise because we didn't know where they had the artillery from to actually reach that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, the sentence I read to you says, Commander Uzelac reports, that 100 of the shells were fired on the forward line of brigade defences. So are you saying that on the morning of the 4th, by 8.00 a.m., you were not told that your forces on the front-lines had come under artillery fire in the 92nd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why these 92nd Motorised Brigade should send a report to me, the Main Staff. That is illogical. It had no business sending me reports. We did not liaise in that way. Perhaps it was as is written in this document, but there was no logic for that to be sent to me. He had his own corps commander. I put things in order there, so one couldn't just, you know, tug the commander by the sleeve as they pleased.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have Exhibit 65 ter 1D1048, please. If we could have page 5 in the English, please, which I believe is page 18 -- 6, page 6 in the B/C/S, please. Now, this -- if we go to the top so you can see the date. Mr. Registrar, if we could go to page 17 in this document. That is the original in the B/C/S. In the B/C/S, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you see the date in the upper left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is that your signature and stamp there?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the signature is mine. Mine is a simple signature, so I don't see what is at issue here. What is the question, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, on the 4th of August, it purports that you're sending a request to the chiefs of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army, asking for replenishment of ammunition, and it's itemised as to what you're seeking on the 4th. Do you recall asking the Yugoslav Army for all of this additional ammunition?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, I do not recall that. This was an insignificant matter for me. This was a technical thing, because the logistics people would issue these requests, and of course they would expect the itemised items to arrive. And perhaps since the combat had already started, they gave it to me to sign. Otherwise, it would be normally signed by Bjelanovic. Why I signed it and if I signed it, I really do not recall, but it is, of course, a normal thing to replenish equipment and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you have -- for example, 27 talks about rockets for an Oganj, you've got shells for an M-55, shells for T-34s, other types of artillery. Let me just ask the question. Did you have --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twenty-seven, it is not Orkan, the rocket is Oganj, the ones they used to pound us in Knin, Oganj, fire, meaning fire. These are 128-millimetre rockets. I did have the Orkans also. And I have 70 pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you're hearing. I said Oganj. I said Oganj. Let me just ask the question. I don't know what you heard.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was maybe misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In the Knin area, where was your artillery deployed?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the artillery, the Main Staff's artillery, was deployed in the area of Slunj, towards Petrova Gora, so that it was able to open fire. It was not in Knin. In Knin, there was the corps artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I meant the 7th Knin Corps. Where was the artillery of the 7th Knin Corps deployed?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we saw that we were threatened and in danger, it was oriented towards Zadar and Split to protect those directions. When the situation changed, we pulled out a portion of the artillery, and that artillery opened fire. When the forces were brought in and when Grahovo was conquered. So we opened fire at Grahovsko Polje, and also from the positions, lower positions to Kninsko Polje. These were Howitzers mostly, there were just two pieces, very few, in fact. And, in fact, we did not manage to pull them out. You captured them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Where is Kninsko Polje, if you can explain that to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was somewhere under Crvena Zemlja, so that it would be within range. We pulled out a couple of pieces there in order to be able to open fire and to support the forces that were defending the decent from Grahovo to Knin. But all this was being addressed prior to the attack, prior to the 4th, and the fighting actually did not start on the 4th. It started -- it had started much earlier. In fact, I believe that there was a bus that had been blown up by a mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But on the 4th itself -- even though the fire started before the 4th, on the 4th itself, were those positions in Kninsko Polje returning the artillery fire? Were they returning fire on Croatian positions?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that artillery had already been pulled up there. As the units moved, as the people moved, it was pulled up towards Otric. It was in no position to be captured down there, and if something was captured, I don't know. That was at the corps level, and I couldn't interfere in their matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, why would you need replenishment of artillery if it's not being used?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Replenishment of artillery was necessary because artillery was used before, in July, when the Sabre action was effected in Western Bosnia, and it started with Polje, because from that time I always had to assist Republika Srpska with a company or two and with ammunition. Ammunition was expended in this way, so I had to seek replenishment to be able to actually properly respond in a war situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to ask that this page be marked, and I tender it into evidence. I note that this is part of a larger 65 ter, and so we will just upload the page that I've used for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it's a bit confusing, this document, the original being far larger than the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I see that, for example, that this page we're talking about appears apparently twice in different formats; once in Cyrillic, with -- but approximately the same content, but without handwriting, et cetera; one's in Latin script. It's a bit confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: These are original documents attached to an overall assessment and analysis that had been prepared, so what you're reading in the Latin script is simply a part of what was an analysis done on those documents. And that's why I flipped to the original document which were actually annexes to the main document. I don't want the main document; I just want the original annex and the translation of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, nevertheless, 11 pages in translation and 21 pages in the original always creates confusion. But if we limit ourselves to what we have on our screen now, technical ways of limiting it to that can be found. Mr. Registrar, that was page 17 in the -- e-court page 17 in the original and - what was the page - 5, I think, in the English. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like the opportunity just to determine -- I'm not going to object to this particular page coming in. I just want the opportunity to put in additional pages from the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's my intention as well, is to use additional pages, but just to break them up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for this moment, page 17, B/C/S, page 5 in the English, where the translation to English also reflects handwritten notes on page 17. Mr. Registrar, limit it to this specific page.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1517.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1517 is admitted into evidence. Could you take care that it's split up?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, was it the usual practice that the Yugoslav Army would supply you with ammunition?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, had some own production for 120-millimetre mortars in Lika, in Licki Osijek, but that was insignificant, so we had to rely on replenishment of purchases on the world market. Mostly the government of the Ministry of the Defence would secure the funds or the resources for that was to be sent to us. As for the Yugoslav Army, they would make available the facilities of -- the production facilities and help us, thus, replenish our expended resources. Otherwise, we would not have been able to survive, and that is no secret, just as Herceg-Bosna would not have been able to survive with the ammunition and the financial resources coming from the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to page 7 in the same document that's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Seven in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, which should then be the next document in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is now a report from you at 1600 hours on the 4th to the Yugoslav Army General Staff, 2nd Administration. Do you recall sending such a report at 1600?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, first, can you tell us why, in the midst of combat operations, you're sending a report to the chief of the Yugoslav Army General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not send him the report because we expected any assistance from him, but so as -- in order for him to be able to acquaint the political leadership of Serbia with the situation and about what was going on. They were surprised. They should not have been surprised. They all pretended to be surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's go to paragraph 2 of your report, and at 1600 you reported: "Our forces were ready for the beginning of the aggression. Despite the inconsiderate activities on all of the towns, the work of the commands of all levels was characterized by calmness."

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "All attacks were stopped." If we go down one sentence -- two sentences : "In the course of the first ten hours of combat, the defence was successfully supported by our aviation and artillery." Now, was that an accurate statement at the time you made it, that you were defending with the use of both aviation and artillery?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for aviation, I don't recall whether it shelled any targets or not or whether it was being re-based because of the danger that it would be within the range of Croatian artillery, so it had to relocate to Banja Luka. The aviation, that took place before the start of the aggression, and that was at the request of UNPROFOR and NATO. I forbade, let me tell you honestly, aviation to open fire on Krk, the fuel depots, and some strategic facilities in Croatia, because I thought that that would amount to pure retaliation, and I did not want to do that because I was guided by International Humanitarian Law. And what they had done, I mean the aviation, they did it prior to the 4th. I would not let Orkans open fire on either Kutina or Zagreb. I sent them off to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is one of those answers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you referred to 1600 hours twice, whereas the stamp at the bottom, as far as I can see, gives "1500 hours."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking Mr. Misetic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see what I signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at the first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's a stamp, "Received 1500 hours."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I confused it with the next document, which is the operative report of 1600 hours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's now corrected and on the record. This document was received at 1500 hours. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. We'll get to 1600 hours with my next document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's at 1500 hours, and if we go to -- but let me ask you again, and let me just -- what I was going to tell you, General, is again, just to remind you to focus your answer on my question, because you may have to stay here longer if we don't get shorter answers. So my question simply is: You've answered the part about the aviation. Were you defending with the use of artillery?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but only against what was endangering us, the forces that we could see, that we could observe. And I issued such assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's go to the next section there: "Artillery activities on towns have caused great destruction and damage." Where was the great destruction? What town had great destruction in it?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is probably an expression someone used in their report. You know how it goes. When reports are being drawn up, you always opt for the augmentative. I was only briefed that all settlements, all inhabited places in the municipality, all towns were shelled. That was not logical, rather than pounding the front, they were opening firing at villages where there were no combatants. Now, had some roofs caved in, had some buildings taken hits, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, we saw the report of General Kovacevic, and you do -- do you dispute General Kovacevic's report that the forces of the 7th Corps on the Dinara were under intense artillery fire there on the front-line?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not dispute that. In fact, I personally observed it, watched it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the next section, and here's what I'm interested in. You report -- as the Presiding Judge has pointed out, 1500 hours is the stamp: "The enemy is conducting a forceful attack from Grahovo over Dinara" --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it's under the paragraph that begins: "At 1100 hours ..." So it's the paragraph in your version that says: "By 1430 hours ..." Do you see that right above the section that -- right above section 3?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Above the decision? Yes, I see it. Yes, the danger is there, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So sometime between 1430 and 1500, you sent a report to Belgrade saying that there was now a breach at Crvena Zemlja and that this breach was putting in danger the defence of Knin; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to break these up, just as I did with the last document, so I would like to mark this -- these pages as a separate exhibit and tender them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I have no objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I see the last page? You never show me the last page. You always show me just the first page, and that is not the document in its entirety. Let me see what I signed, if it is not too much trouble for the technician to show it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the original be shown to the witness, the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This should be also read: "We feel that all necessary measures must urgently be taken to stop the Croatian aggression." So war was not our objective. Our objective was a peaceful resolution of the situation, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, you were asked whether you could see the second page to see whether this is what you signed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were not invited to comment on the document. If there is any relevance, then Mr. Russo might ask questions about it to you, or any of the other Defence counsel. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, I don't think we've got a number. And just for the record, these pages are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, you're right, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The pages are page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just for the purposes of the record, Mr. President, this is pages 18 and 19 of the B/C/S and pages 7 and 8 of the English.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, those will become Exhibit D1518.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to the next pages in this series.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is a report from, again, Lieutenant-Colonel Mihajlo Knezevic, and he's sending a report to the Yugoslav Army General Staff, 2nd Administration, with an operative time of 1600 hours, and the stamp says: "Received at 1645." Now, what I'm interested in, in this report, is in the third paragraph. He now reports on the axis Grahovo-Crvena Zemlja-Knin: "The Ustasha have succeeded in taking over the dominant peaks and creating favourable conditions for the continuation of their activities and breaking out to the immediate vicinity of Knin." Now, can you recall if, at approximately 1600 hours, the situation was now such that the Croatian Army had broken through and had taken up positions that were now favourable for the advancement on Knin? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, and the MUP pulled out. They got scared. They avoided a frontal engagement, direct engagement. They could have -- the forces could have entered Knin immediately after the pullout, had they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now if we look down two paragraphs, he also reports: "They have succeeded around 1500 hours to take over the Mali Alan ridge on The mount Velebit and jeopardised the Celavac TV transmitter." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And is that correct, in terms of the timing, that it's around 1500 hours where there was a breakthrough on the Velebit side towards Gospic?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was -- the communications were severed and the lines were down. I had no communication at all with the corps commander, except the previous concept that I had issued to them in the preparation stage. But I believe that repeater was shelled by NATO aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But let me make sure you answered my question. Is it correct, as reported here, that approximately 1500 hours it was reported that the Croatian Army had broken through at Mali Alan and was now threatening Gracac?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So is it correct, based on what you testified yesterday, that as of 1600 hours on the 4th, based on the breakthroughs up on Crvena Zemlja and from this side, from the coastal side at Mali Alan, that this threatened encirclement was now possible?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, and realistically that was this major risk, major danger for this entire region of Dalmatia, to be cut off and to remain part of Croatia, which would have been all right except for the fact that there was the danger of people getting killed at the hands of the different paramilitary units and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that pages -- page 20 and 21 -- oh, I'm sorry, page 20 of the B/C/S and page -- pages 9 and 10 of the English be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, these two pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, those will become Exhibit D1519.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could I have Exhibit D927 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. -- I'm sorry, General, do you recall in the late afternoon, sometime after 4.00, being on a phone call with Milan Babic in Belgrade, you and Mr. Martic being on a phone call with Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that, while the communications were still functional.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you, first, tell us, from your own memory, what was discussed in that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain. I didn't talk to him, personally. It was the president of the republic talking to the prime minister. We sent the prime minister there to go there to see that everything is done in order for war to be averted, to talk to people in the American Embassy, sign all variants of the plans, the Z-4 and what have you, just so as to avert war. So when we finished the session of the Main Staff of the Supreme Command, where we had ministers, the president of the Assembly, the minister of the interior, and this was in the operations conference room of the Main Staff, we arrived at an assessment, and you can see that also on the basis of these documents, to the effect that there was the danger of forces penetrating through Crvena Zemlja into Knin whenever they so wished and that they cut off the line at Otric, cut off the whole of Dalmatia, because nobody was attacking from up there. So a political decision needed to be made. We were unable to make such a decision on our own. We had to consult all the members of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the screen here and see if the details here -- this again is a recording of that telephone conversation, and it says -- it starts off with you and Mr. Babic, General Mrksic and Milan, and it says -- number 1 is Mr. Babic, number 2 is you. Number 1 says: "It's like this, I talked to --" Well, if this can make refresh your recollection. It says -- and Mr. Martic -- let me just -- you haven't had a chance to read it? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now I'm looking at it, but this is not Mile Mrksic; this is not the style of Mile Mrksic. I just do not allow that this is the way I express myself. I'm not a man who uses cunt words. Whoever prepared this for you planted this. I'm [Realtime transcript read in error "I'm not"] a guards officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said it was -- number 1 is Mr. Babic. Where do we find that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: A certain Milan, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A certain Milan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You make it Mr. Babic, which still has to be established. It should not be put to the witness in a way --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the document does not appear in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's just that there are three Milans on this conversation, Mr. President, and it's going to be difficult to keep them all straight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But let's try to follow this, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, is there anything of concern?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Just an intervention. In the transcript, on page 11: "I'm not a guards officer." Mr. Mrksic actually said, "I am" or "I was a guards officer," not "I'm not."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's -- and you may not be familiar with the rules that apply in this court. If you think that the transcript or the translation presents something which is not accurate, then you're not supposed to give your own opinion on what would be accurate, but you can question the matter, see when it's a matter of translation; to seek first the witness to repeat his answer. If it's a matter of transcription, and to point at the page and the line where you think there is any inaccuracy. But it is the habit in this courtroom that we do not replace what we think to be wrong by what we think to be right. It's on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My suggestion would be that we take a break, and I will give the witness a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that the witness can read it during the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, we have some homework for you. Mr. Misetic will have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- will hand you a hard copy of the transcript of this recorded telephone conversation. If you'd please be so kind to read it over the break. We'll then have a break and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, have you had a chance to review that transcript of a telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not interested in word for word right now, that you go through it and say every word is correct. Just if you could tell the Court, before you saw that, you said there was a conversation with Mr. Babic and that it was related to this decision on whether to issue an evacuation order. Just by looking at that, in terms of refreshing your recollection, can you tell the Court either what -- I'm sorry. Can you tell the Court what specifically was discussed with Mr. Babic prior to the decision to issue the evacuation order?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, let me say that as far as I can recall, I did not have a conversation with Mr. Babic; rather, that was the task of the president of the republic, Martic. I was never referred to as Milan in any conversation. My name is Mile Mrksic. And even looking at this conversation, no one would have said "Milan." Especially there wouldn't be a conversation of this time with the prime minister because I didn't even know him. But I do know that there was a phone conversation or, as they said, a phone session, because they needed to consult him as a member of the Supreme Command as to what to do next.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What were you told was discussed with Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the republic said that he had consultations with him and that they agreed, that he had proposed -- that he had put forward a proposal, and this was the opinion of the staff, that people should not be left to their own devices and at the mercy of whoever, that they should be removed from Krajina to Srb. There was no mention of abandoning or leaving the territory of Republika Srpska. This is what we called the tactical and operational movement. But of course there is always a danger when people get in motion, because our people were armed, the population was armed because that was the concept of our defence, and we were aware that there might be problems with that. Following this, there was probably a decision that was probably signed by the president or I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether there was any discussion -- I'm sorry. Just for purposes of the transcript, if I could ask you -- there may have been something missed in the interpretation. You said the people should not be left to their own devices. What was the -- what was the fear or what was the motivation?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be honest, there was a historic -- a historical fear that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think you already answered it, but let me ask it this way: This decision, was it because of the danger that there was going to be an encirclement?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That decision was made because of the danger of encirclement, and we were not sure that the treatment of the civilian population would be fair and that there would follow what we expected, disarming people and then deciding who is guilty and who is not. And then there was also a great fear regarding Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What was the fear regarding Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people were afraid of the force that was then displayed by the Croatian government. Next, there were victims that should not have been there. As it turned out, there were casualties, and those people who did not want to leave the area, who did not want to withdraw to a safer area. I believe the then forces of the Republic of Croatia were not capable of controlling their own forces, and there are always extremists who could -- who could wreak havoc among on people and who could harm people. And, of course, people were afraid. And what do you think? If everybody had remained behind, do you have any idea what the number of victims would have been? This way, only the old people remained and those people who had no means to move out of there, because there was no one to take them out of there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether it was reported to you that Mr. Babic conveyed in that conversation whether you could expect assistance from Mr. Galbraith or the international community?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he had contacts with Martic. And what I can see here, I think that's what it refers to, that there was no assistance to be expected and that once this started, there is no -- there was no way of stopping it anymore. It couldn't even be stopped in Geneva. Mr. Cervenko wouldn't come and talk to me. When that happened, it was clear to me that this decision had been made and there was no stopping it anymore. And, of course, it was in our interests to prevent that. And I think President Milosevic was cheated out of this and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. This conversation is purported to be at 1630. And if we could now go to Exhibit D137, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, is that taken from the code at the top, which ends with "1630?" I'm not -- I don't know whether we had paid any attention to what this code --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's the time, as far as I understand, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If that's not in dispute, then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, General, this is a document that's been admitted into evidence as the evacuation order that was issued by Mr. Martic. Do you recall seeing this document before?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I see this document, but I am aware that he did issue this document. I haven't read it before, but I know that it was drafted in keeping with decisions at the sessions of the Supreme Council. It probably came to the staff and was probably filed there, but because I participated in the session, there was no need to show it to me. And now I see that this is a short order consisting of three points.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First, if you look at the time in the upper left-hand corner, is that time consistent with your recollection that the order was issued at 1645; in other words, sometime after the conversation with Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can see at the bottom there that this was actually certified, that only at 5.20 it was actually distributed. You can see that at the bottom of the page, because it takes time to type this and then file it, and so on. So this was issued as a result of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, can you explain to us why the Main Staff had to certify it?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the president of the republic is the supreme commander, and he sat in sessions of the Main Staff. He was our boss, in fact. He was a member of the Main Staff, and all the decisions that were made, he presided over them. And, of course, he used, in wartime, the administration and everything. He was not physically with the Presidency. Whether he had also brought with him somebody else from the Presidency to the Main Staff, I can't recall, because the premises where the Main Staff was were also the premises for the MUP and the Main Staff of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At your answer on page 44, line 21, you said "only at 5.20 was it actually distributed." Can you tell us to whom it was distributed?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report was only sent to the brigades to which it refers, and the municipalities to which it refers, so the Dalmatia Corps, the Benkovac, Obrovac, and Drnis Brigades, and Obrovac and Gracac. It did not relate to Lika, Kordun or Banija; only the area that we discussed a few days ago that could be cut off and encircled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, then, this order was passed down through the military line?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how this was done, technically. This is actually taken by courier. I don't know if it was taken to the municipal bodies, whether from there somebody else distributed it further. I don't know what the actual technology is and how the civilian authorities handled this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: Do you know who Drago Kovacevic is?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was the president of Knin --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- as far as I can recall. But this was a long time ago, so I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if Mr. Kovacevic was present at the meeting where the decision was taken to issue the evacuation order?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall, but it would have been a good thing had he been there. It would be normal, because it was his corps, the people from his corps. I can't recall. I can't remember the people and every detail, especially because I didn't really spend much time there, and I didn't know the people too well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, do you recall whether you walked into that meeting and said that the evacuation should go to Petrovac and Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Why would I alter the decision of the Supreme Council? I didn't have the authority to do that, and why would I do it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me show you a video-clip and ask you to watch it, and then I'll ask for your comment after the clip. This is, Mr. Registrar, Exhibit D326.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Refugee columns were travelling through Knin at a large scale when, at approximately 5.00 p.m. on 4 August 1995, representatives of the civilian and military authorities met at Martic's headquarters. And Martic, who was in uniform, there was a huge ashtray in front of him, several empty packs of cigarettes, and then we exchanged hellos. And on the topic of why he had called me, he said he called me because, he said, I've decided to evacuate the city, and we should take steps to relocate the civilian population, I must stress this, civilian population from Northern Dalmatia, meaning from the municipalities of Benkovac, Obrovac, Knin, Drnis, and from the municipality of Gracac in Lika." "This did not come as a shock to me. I perceived this to be some sort of rational measure. At that moment, we passed the order. It was Kosta Novakovic specifically who passed the order. It was then that we wrote in the order that this was to evacuate the civilian population, meaning in the direction of Knin, Otric, or Srb or Lapac, which were the areas where people were to be relocated. It was then that Mrksic reacted and said, What do you mean by Srb? We need to go further than Srb, towards Petrovac and Banja Luka. And then he cautioned us that if the civilians embark on leaving, that the military lines would be at risk. He said the civilians start, then the army goes after them to evacuate them, and this is going to create enormous problems. "However, sometime during the evening, when he arrived, he was upstairs, Mrksic. He told me on the staircase that the evacuation of the population had been ordered. I told him, General, the army will break down. What do you mean by evacuating the people, and this means of an order? He said, This is not in our hands. It was the Supreme Defence Council decision. And then someone had requested that Martic -- or it was Martic himself who had requested to be put through to Slobo Milosevic, but he did not speak with him. Rather, he spoke with Brane Crncic [phoen]. So he got hold of Brane Crncic, probably because he couldn't get hold of Slobo. He assured him that probably he couldn't -- so that's why he spoke to Brane, and then he was told by him, No, no, he won't take any steps, the Slobo wouldn't do anything in this case.
