And it was then for the first-time I heard it was then that Martic cursed Slobo, and so on and so forth."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mrksic, let me just give you an opportunity to comment on Mr. Kovacevic's version of events. Did you, in fact, state that, We have to go farther than this order and we have to go to Petrovac and Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Mr. Kovacevic was saying there, I don't even remember that he was there, nor did I go where that full ashtray full of ashes were. We -- what Kosta said in that sense, we knew of that, and that's what was said. But that I should have said that they should move on and go further, no, I could not possibly have said that, nor was it in keeping with the assignment that I was given by President Milosevic when I was sent to Krajina, nor would I ever order such a thing. Whether this is some sort of game where someone is trying to impugn the General Mrksic order or something, that's different, but my order was not to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me now show you three additional documents. I will show them to you one at a time. And in order to save time, I'll give you an opportunity to comment on them after we've looked at all three. Okay? First, if we could turn to Exhibit D182. Now, I'll give you an opportunity to comment, but later in more detail. But if you could just answer me "yes" or "no." Are you aware that there was a meeting held at 1800 hours with the UNPROFOR or UNCRO command headquarters? Are you aware of that? Just "yes" or "no," and I'll give you an opportunity later to comment further.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall. It's possible, but I can't recall. But I believe if I don't recall it, I probably did not attend that meeting. I don't know. Because the situation was critical, it was very difficult, who was doing what and when and how.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, you told us that you have no recollection, and you think, having no recollection, that you would not have been present. That's an answer to the question. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, at that meeting, where the evacuation was discussed? In other words, the council, the Defence Council, was it discussed at that meeting, that UNCRO Command should be approached in order to assist with the evacuation? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether Kosta Novakovic was issued such an assignment, I don't know, because he was the liaison, but I can't really remember. We sought help wherever we could find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me show you now these three documents, and then I'll give you an opportunity to comment. This is -- the first is -- I believe it's UNCRO, a report sent at 1945. Do not pay attention to the date, because everyone in this case agrees that the date should be 4 August 1995. Now, if you look at the second paragraph here, it says: "The RSK authorities have requested UN assistance in organising and providing transport for such evacuation. RSK initial calculation shows that UN will need to provide for these refugees transportation, around 70.000 litres of fuel and 450 trucks. RSK proposed one main route, Knin-Padjene-Otric-Srb-Martin Brod-Bosanski Petrovac-Banja Luka." Now, let me turn to Exhibit D337, please. And if we could go to page 2, paragraph 4. D337, General Mrksic, is a report from Yasushi Akashi to Kofi Annan on the evening of the 4th of August. And at paragraph 4, in the first sentence, he says: "We have been advised by the Civil Affairs Office in Sector South that the Knin leadership have requested UNHCR and UNPF assistance in evacuating approximately 32.000 civilians from Benkovac, Obrovac, Gracac, and Knin to Petrovac and Banja Luka in Bosnia and Herzegovina." Finally, let me show you 65 ter 172, and these are the personal notes of a gentleman named Drago Vujatovic, and he took handwritten notes at the meeting with the UNCRO command. And if we go to English page 16, please. If we go to the bottom. He notes the meeting started at 1740. Kosta Novakovic is present, K. Milan, K. Drago, and then it's noted: "Alain Forand; Mrksic, Mile; Trbulin, Milan." If we turn the page, please, in English. Let me -- I'm sorry, I don't think we have shown it to you in the original. It's page 129 in the B/C/S. Okay. Right in that middle of the page are his handwritten notes, and then it says, if we turn the page in English, which we have, okay, he wrote in hand: "EV. Knin-Benkovac-Obrovac-Drnis-Gracac-Otric-Srb-Lapac, defend ..." Then something about: " ... Galbraith is requesting from Tudjman." Then: "Martin Brod further on to Banja Luka, drive to the end." And if we scroll down a bit, and also scroll down in the B/C/S, he says: "Martin Brod-Petrovac-Banja Luka," and then: "Fuel." And there's a breakdown of 15.000 and then, overall, 32.000. And 32.000, you'll recall, is the same number that Mr. Akashi reports as the number of people that were going to be moving out of these areas. Now, first, were you present at this meeting? Does this refresh your recollection at all as to whether you were present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. This is the first time I hear this; this the first time I see this. To the best of my recollection, I was not there. And I only had meetings with Akashi, and when delegations from the United Nations came, as well as with the -- and I never had a meeting with a local UNPROFOR commander there, as far as I can recall. And as for these things here, this is the first time that I see this. I cannot help you any there. I can only confirm what the president signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation as to why representatives of the RSK, at a meeting that took place apparently less than an hour after Mr. Martic issued the evacuation order, why they would go to this meeting and say that they would drive on to Petrovac or Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to object. That calls for speculation as to what's in the minds of other individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, sometimes other individuals -- perhaps you could ask him whether he received any information which could shed some light on why others may have said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you have such information?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not participate in it. But now I'm placing myself in the role of an ordinary man in the street, of an ordinary peasant. The more he can get, the more inventive he will be. He will ask for more fuel, for more assistance. This is the psychology of our folk. It wasn't an official position. It wasn't my official position, or that of the president, or of anybody else. It is a fact that later matters evolved so that the people had to withdraw from the area, and the area became too cramped, too constricted, for such a large number of people, and there was the pressure being exerted on them. There was the danger that they would get killed. The question to be asked is, why was this set in motion, not how did it evolve.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that 65 ter -- I ask that 65 ter 172 be marked and ask that it be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: There's no objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1520.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, General Mrksic, do you recall having a meeting with your subordinates at 2000 hours on the 4th of August in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall a meeting that was to address the military issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to jog my memory to tell me what the agenda was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me show you two reports that you've seen already earlier. But to jog your memory, let's see if this will help. Exhibit D1516, please. If we could go -- I'm sorry. This is the report of General Kovacevic of the 9th of August that you saw earlier today. And if we could go to page 2 in the English of this and paragraph 6. Now, General Kovacevic reports: "On 4 August, at 2000 hours, the SVK commander issued the order for the reinforcement of the defence of Knin by taking out one infantry battalion from the 75th Motorised Brigade, while the remaining units should be engaged in defence at their current positions, at the same time organising decisive defence at the line ..." And then it identifies the line. It says: "In the course of 4 August, the RSK government issued a public statement, calling the entire population in the endangered areas to evacuate, which caused a chaos within the units and their dispersion, because the soldiers started leaving in order to go home and help their families with the evacuation." Now if we could go to Exhibit D828, please. This is, I'm going to show you, Mr. Uzelac's report of the 92nd Motorised Brigade. If we could go to B/C/S page 2 and English page 3 of this report. Now, I'm interested in, if we could scroll down again, at 1900 hours: "At 1900 hours, we received an instruction from the authorities that it is necessary to do an evacuation of the civilian population. We transfer the order to persons in charge of evacuation. "At 1905, I leave for the Main Staff in Knin. At the KM at 2000 hours, with the presence of the brigade commanders of the Command of the Main Staff and commander of the 7th Knin Corps, whom I meet for the first time, we are informed by Main Staff Commander General Mrksic of the situation in the RSK in the area of Kordun, Banija, Lika, especially the area of responsibility of the 7th Corps, that the situation is very complex, that the Vrlika Brigade is under attack, that the Ustasha in the 2nd Infantry Brigade have taken Cista Mala and Cista Velika. The authorities are not functioning, et cetera. He orders that the area of responsibility of the corps ..." If we could turn the page in English, please: " ... is reduced, that the areas of responsibility of brigades are reduced, and that the general situation is borne in mind. "I reacted and warned the commander that the 92nd Motorised Brigade was holding its positions firmly. There has been fighting, but there have not been any successes by the Ustashas in my area. I am ready to fight back any attack. I told him that no civilians had been evacuated from Benkovac. I suggest that all commanders be persistent in defending their areas, that conditions be provided for evacuation of civilians, that the super-ordinate commands ensure forces for stopping Ustashas from the direction of Vrlika-Knin." If we could go to the next page in the B/C/S, please: "At 2300 at the KM of the 92nd Motorised Brigade in Gornje Biljane, I introduce everybody to the situation in the RSK, especially the 7th Corps, and ask them all for suggestions. We were all utterly shocked by what was happening. There had been hundreds of attacks on the brigade area of responsibility, and we were not scared by the Ustashas. "I order the units: Defend the areas of defence; take actions toward Ustashas on certain directions in order to display activity; prevent any infiltration or spiking; make possible the pullout of civilians from the front-line." Now, General, first, does this refresh your recollection about what was discussed at the meeting at 2000? That's "yes"?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do remember we discussed these matters. Now, whether it was exactly in this way or not, I'm not sure, but we talked about it, and mainly with the commanders of the 7th Dalmatia Corps. Because if the people pulled out, why should they hold such a wide front? They should, in fact, protect the area where the people would arrive. And, of course, there were comments of this kind, and some people did not quite understand the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Why did you feel it necessary to shorten the front?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that the front should be shortened because there was no one up there in that area. One could ascend that portion from Knin, and whom were the troops to defend if the people had moved out and there were no forces to confront there at that time? It was a bit more difficult for the commanders to comprehend because they had already prepared their fortifications, their entrenchments, and everything, but there were no forces attacking them there. The attack was coming from the territory of Republika Srpska. So this is what gave rise to this entire agenda. We knew in advance that there would be a problem if the people left and the combatants remained, because they would go to their own homes and seek to protect their own families. But the political decisions were made along these lines; namely, had they actually decided that we should fight within the encirclement, I would have implemented such a task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, then, based on this last answer, that what was happening was those who were holding their lines, nevertheless, you were concerned that they would be attacked from behind because of the penetration by the HV in Knin and Mali Alan?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, because to hold the lines, the old lines, in the front of Benkovac-Velika-Drnis, would mean nothing if the front was from behind. We had to set up a new front in order to stop those forces from penetrating into the region of Otric and this other area where the people were located. We were an armed people, and our task was not to defend territory but to defend the people, to prevent the people from coming to harm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall any discussion about Bulina Strana at this meeting at 2000?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is probably the exit from Knin, Bulina Strana. I've forgotten those names. Yes, we talked about that. That is the key feature to prevent them from going up, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is what I mean. And if we can explain to the Court what you mean geographically. Bulina Strana is what in relation to Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a map now. This is a feature up there where the road to Otric leads. That was the position of the forward command post of the Knin Corps, and I sent the president of the republic there to rest a bit and so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, to speed this up, I don't think it will be in dispute that Bulina Strana is at an elevation in relation to Knin town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me without my having a map in front of me. And so much time has elapsed, I know where the salient features are; Petrova Gora, Dinara and so on. But for these hillocks, I would have to look at a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll get to that --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I ordered some forces to be up there, that means that it was significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I think you touched on it in your answer, and let me ... You said, at page 56, line 23, that: "Bulina Strana was the key feature to prevent them from going up, if that's what you mean." Can you explain that a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is this, please show me, so that I can read the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's on the transcript. Part of your answer today, to my question a few minutes ago, was that, in terms of importance of Bulina Strana, "it was a key feature to prevent them," meaning the HV, "from going up."

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to look at a map, if this is above Knin, where the railway track is, where the railway station is, where the road leading to Otric and Lika is, and then that is it. This is where the main defence should have been. That is where we should have prevented them from striking at the people. That is where the fighting should have been. That is what I meant, if that is what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think maybe it will be easier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, from the answer of the witness, it was clear that he was uncertain about names. That appears on 56:23. And then he continued, we talked about that, and at the same time he says that he doesn't know the names anymore. So, therefore, it might be not fully accurate to present, as part of his answer, that this happened at Bulina Strana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will show him a different document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But before I get to that, let me show him one other document on the evacuation. This is 65 ter 1D1057.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And this is the report, General Mrksic, of the commander of the 15th Lika Corps, yes, the Lika Corps, Stevo Sevo. And I just want to go to page 3 in the English, the portion that says: "On 4 August 1995, around 2330 hours ..." Now -- yes. It says: "Around 2330 hours, the chief of the General Staff of the Serbian Krajina Army personally passed the order to begin the general evacuation of the population in the area of the responsibility of the corps." Now, do you recall issuing -- personally passing such an order?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Chief of the General Staff? No, I never passed any such order. It was the chief of my staff who sent to Loncar, who had a son in the Lika Corps and went to see him and to see what the situation was there, perhaps he did something on his own, at his own initiative like that. I didn't do anything of the kind. And all this was written later in Banja Luka, when everybody was resentful at what had happened, and everybody wrote what they did in hindsight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But, General, I guess my question to you is: Mr. Martic's evacuation order did not cover Lika; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not; it did not. And everything else that was done, that was abuse; namely, it was either my name or his name being abused or misused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: There's no objection, Mr. President. However, I would just like to correct the record with respect to the representation made about that the evacuation did not cover Lika.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He confirmed it in his answer, that it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I think the document shown to the witness, D137, indicates parts of Lika.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was put to the witness. The question is answered by the witness. Whether it's consistent with other pieces of evidence, we'll evaluate that when looking at the evidence in its entirety. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit D1521.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have Exhibit D713 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, General Mrksic, do you recall going on Radio Belgrade on the evening of the 4th of August, giving a report to Radio Belgrade about the situation in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not my custom to give statements to either radio or television. I don't remember. Perhaps if someone had interviewed me or just talked to me and then recorded it and broadcast it on television. I, personally, do not recall having made any such statement, or I haven't heard that, that I spoke on radio or television. I would like to read that to see what it is that you're talking about. This is news to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you've answered the question. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First, this is one version of that, and this is reported carried in the archives of BBC summary of world broadcasts. And the source, the fourth line, says: "Serbian Radio Belgrade in Serbo-Croat, 2000 hours GMT," which is 2200 hours Central European Time, "4 August 1995." And the second paragraph -- and I will show you a different version of this so that you can follow it, but it says: "A telephone interview with General Milan Mrksic, commander of the Serb Krajina Army in Knin ..." And if I can show you a different exhibit of the same interview. Mr. Registrar, this is D106, please. Now, this quotes you as saying first: "At present, all combat activities in the area of Knin have ceased. Knin is enveloped by the dark; evacuation of the population is ongoing. Enemy forces reached at four to six kilometres from the city of Knin." Then there's a question, and then you're quoted again: "We are maintaining contact; our forces withdrew to the positions for the direct defence of Knin. The other units are still successfully holding their positions." And then the next answer is: "HV was successful on the direction from Grahovo towards Knin. They had success in Velebit, in conquering, in taking of Mali Alan. Furthermore, they were successful, partially, though, in Banija." If we go down a few lines: "There is a danger of splitting apart parts of Krajina. Presently, we are engaged in evacuation of the population from Dalmatia, to prevent them from falling captive, because Knin and the communications leading from Knin are in danger. Persistent defence shall create conditions for that task to be carried out. If the VRS succeeds in putting the pressure on the forces attacking in the direction of Grahovo-Knin, we shall then stabilise the defence and switch on to counter-attack." Now, does that refresh your recollection at all about giving such a statement on Radio Belgrade on the evening of the 4th?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the communications were broken down, and it was impossible to have a conversation after the repeater was struck. It doesn't matter that it's written down here, but I never had -- it was not my custom to give interviews to radio or television. Maybe I had a conversation with someone, but I don't believe that it was possible to maintain communications. But, generally speaking, this actually is consistent with the report to the Corps Command, but I can't tell you exactly whether I did or didn't; I really don't recall. And for me, this is one of those documents that I would like to see. And if you have some more, by all means. But this was not my custom, and I did not -- I never really liked to stand out, nor did I like to pose for photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you, then, the next question. Did you speak with Frenki Simatovic on the evening of the 4th of August via telephone?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see Frenki Simatovic either during the operations in Western Bosnia, nor did I talk to him over the phone, nor did he -- nor was he wont to call me on the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you speak to Jovica Stanisic on the evening of the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have a conversation with Jovica Stanisic because of the state of the communications, but a telegram arrived saying that we should hold on for a couple of days and that the international community would interfere and save Krajina. Well, in that sense, something to that effect, if that's what you're referring to. Maybe you actually have it. It was sort of reassuring or encouragement, but I did not have direct contact with him, nor did I hear his voice or he mine, because Martic could not actually get through to President Milosevic because the lines were down. All I know is that we got news to the effect, Hang in there, hang in there, and something will come about. And, of course, this is natural. I would have done the same thing had I been in Belgrade and somebody else in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us why Jovica Stanisic would be sending you telegrams and giving you advice about holding out?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why. Perhaps this was the political position that the leadership of Serbia took, maybe the president's position and all the other circles, to just hold out for another couple of days and that then the international players would change their attitude towards Croatia and that they would discontinue or stop their advance and proceed to a peaceful resolution, so that all the proposals that were being circulated around, including Z-4 and so on, would come into play. I don't know why this was so, but you should ask him, not me. But I assume that this is what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What was the name of the person nicknamed "Medo" who was an associate of Jovica Stanisic's?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we called him "Medo." That was a nickname that we used, "Medo," because he was rather stout. So we all called him "Medo," or "Teddy bear." I don't know what the names were, because they did not usually use their proper names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court what Medo's role was, who he was in relationship to Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know; I don't know. He was the liaison with Jovica Stanisic, but what his actual function was or what he did, where he was, I never knew this, nor could I ask. They probably had their own assignments. I wouldn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Registrar, could we have Exhibit D441 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is a report which I know you've never seen before because it's a Croatian government report. But if you look at it, it's from the 1st of August, it's within the Special Police Sector. It says: "A Red Beret platoon, Captain Dragan's troops from the centre for the training of special forces in Bruska - have arrived in the Gracac area. "A plan has been made to evacuate the civilian population from the Gracac area via Srb to Republika Srpska." Now, do you recall whether members of the Red Berets were operating in the area of Gracac during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall. I know that the Captain Dragan's centre used to be in Bruska. This was practically a centre for the training of scouts. He was some sort of professional in this field. He trained scouts for manning units. And they were not called the Red Berets. They also had GPS systems. They used all this technology. I wouldn't know anything about what is stated here, Bartele, Bartele, or Medak, or whatever, UNCRO and so on. I wouldn't know anything about this. And I think during -- in my day, when I actually brought in some order, they could not do this, because they had to be within the regime that I had imposed. Well, I would like to say something. I disarmed all "mindjusari" so they could not actually hijack the trucks and so on. I just put in some order and, well, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have on the screen Exhibit D948, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, General, I'm going to read portions of what purports to be an intercepted telephone conversation at 2158 on the 4th of August. The first portion purportedly is between Medo and Zezelj. First, can you tell us who Zezelj was?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This is the first time that I hear that name. There used to be a general of the JNA, Zezelj. He was the Guards Command. He hailed from Lika.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go down. There's a line that says: "M: And where's Mile at? "G: He's here. "M: Put him on." And then the comment here is, in the further course of conversation, he is talking to General Mile Mrksic, who he addresses with Mrkso. Now: "G: Hello, Medo." And then it goes on. If we go down a little bit, it says: "G: The rest considering the battles is fine. There was a little bit something up there in Velebit. Your guys did it well. There is one of your guys wounded up there." And then M responds: "I know, it's two of them. Okay, they will be down there. I'll see you in 24 hours." "G: Well, it's finished here. Knin is being emptied. Relocation is organised." "M: Well, can you go to the city?" "G: Well, we will defend Knin tomorrow, and the day after tomorrow, and any way we can." Now, first, do you recall whether the person you referred to as Medo, the person you referred to as Medo, had sent his own forces near the Velebit area on the 4th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea what the forces -- what the manpower was, nor what his assignment was, nor could Medo address me in this way. I mean, you should proceed from a different position. Had you proceeded from a military stand, perhaps I could come to believe this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's keep going --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, this doesn't make any sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's keep going.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, that he would address me with "Mrkso" and so on, no one ever addressed me that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, on an open line, typically in combat as a military man, would you use your real names and your full titles on an open telephone line?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean did I have a code-name? Well, these commanders would know that. In wartime, during combat, but also in peacetime -- in peacetime, we would use rank and last name, and whereas in wartime we would use a code-name, Lasta, Zemlja, a mountain name, or something of that sort. Everyone would know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In other words, you agree, though, that you wouldn't use your own name, in a war situation, on an open telephone line; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they would use the code-name. The person that I would talk to would know my voice, and there would be no need to actually introduce myself. The commander is here --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then it says: "G: Knin is empty, but we will defend." M says: "Okay, your friends are here at my place, and they want to say hello." And then the comment is: "A friend, X, and Mrksic participate in the further course of conversation."

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: X?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. X says: "Listen, your situation is not as bad as it looks. They didn't do nothing, man." It goes down: "G: Okay, we will fight tomorrow. Just how much forces and assets ..." If we could turn the page in English, please: " ... they spent." X then says: "Well, they can't do it differently. They have to beat -- they have to finish the job quickly. The problem is in Gracac, the valley." "G: I know, man. I sent up there. That has gotten broken over there, and I sent some units there." X then says: "Listen, Crvena Zemlja, that's all slopes. They can't reach you." "G: What do you mean they can't? They are here, they are watching Knin from up there." Then the conversation a few lines down, X says: "Don't wait for him down there, but above Knin. Don't wait for him down there, Mrkso. Mind that you keep Gracac." Okay. Now, let's speak generally first. On the evening of the 4th, why was it important for you to hold on to Gracac?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that yesterday or the day before yesterday. After Gracac fell, the communication towards Srb was in jeopardy, so now there was a possibility to cut off all the forces at that location. But the conversation that you are now referring to -- I'll ask you afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Hold on. Had you held on to Gracac, had you been able to defend Gracac and keep the HV forces from entering Gracac, was it your intention to defend -- was it your intention to defend Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think Gracac, too, fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm saying let's take ourselves back to the evening of the 4th. You're trying to keep the HV out of Gracac. My question to you is --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- had you been able to hold on to Gracac, how would you have defended Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- it was not possible for us to defend Knin and to prevent you from coming in. But we had the possibility of preventing you from advancing from there onwards, and that is why there was this relocation of the 7th Corps, and that is why we brought that unit to Bruvno so that these forces would not enter from the rear, from behind, into Srb. It was all very complicated. When Grahovo fell, the entire defence operation and the concept, the very concept, became very complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page in English, please. Now, there's a line here where G is reported to have said: "Well, F it. The communication assets in Knin are not working. They shot everything this morning. I was left without electricity, TV, radio, everything." Now, I'm just asking you a general question. Were your communication assets damaged on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I just want to raise an objection to the manner in which this exhibit is being used. He's been read several portions of it. He's never been asked if he agrees with this as an accurate representation of a conversation he had. It's being used in an extremely leading manner. I think we should just ask the witness, in fairness, if it represents a conversation he was a part of or if he's aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think he's stated that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That question was asked to him. He commented on it, rather than directly answering that question, and that gives a bit of an ambiguous picture. And then I think what Mr. Misetic did is to ask him questions about matters that are also discussed in the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. And, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, Mr. Misetic, I'd certainly encourage you to deal with the matters also without having read greater portions of the conversation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President. My intention, of course, is that, to the extent it will be an issue, that the Chamber is entitled to assess the probative value based on whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber always is. That is not an answer to any way of how to proceed during examination, but it goes without saying that the Chamber finally will --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying is to the extent that, generally speaking a witness says that matters discussed in here are consistent otherwise with his recollection, it tends to increase the probative value of the document, but that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you could also ask him some matters without first referring to the television conversation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And also for the record, Mr. President, it's my understanding that this document is -- its authenticity is not disputed and it's being used by the Prosecution in other matters, but I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I don't believe that's the issue, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. At the same time, it's not totally unrelated. If you consider this to be a conversation by certain persons, and then to say, Well, the witness could -- we always took that view, but now the witness takes a different position, so therefore that's all not valid anymore, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Just to be clear, Mr. President, I don't believe there's been prior testimony about who the actual participants are. The document purports to indicate whomever wrote the transcript believes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that the content of these documents gives some clues as to who they might be, but perhaps we should make that perhaps more explicit. And if an answer would be that, It's unimaginable that someone would address me like this and that, that nevertheless can have happened. So therefore perhaps to take a more factual approach in follow-up questions if the witness has said anything about his participation in a conversation which is transcribed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I believe I've asked him, generally speaking, on both conversations, but let me ask these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, other than Frenki --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Other than Frenki Simatovic, do you know any other person named Frenki?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I maintain that I cannot admit to having participated in this conversation at all. I don't know this document. It's totally foreign to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask the next question. Other than Jovica Stanisic, in 1995 did you have -- did you know anyone named Jovica who was in any position of authority in Yugoslavia, Republika Srpska, or the Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean someone significant, a person of significance? No, I did not know any other significant person by that name. I mean, if it were an important person, I would have remembered. But you were going to ask me about the electric power and things like that. What is it, you've given up on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No. My colleagues do a good job sometimes of distracting me from the issue. So, please, tell us what happened to your communications on 4 August.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of NATO strikes and their actions from the ships, and because of electronic jamming, and the generals here will know of that, because I had old equipment, since 1.00 or 2.00 p.m. on the 4th, I had no type -- no communications assets at all, except the conceptual communication, like we did in the partisan days. The TV was cut off. There was no power. There was some new TV sender. Everything was the same, but the reporters were different. There were new TV stations, propaganda. I was proclaimed to be dead. My mother was bereaved, and my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, General: Part of your communications, did they go through the PTT?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The post and telecommunications was down. There was only connection with Lapac. There was a railway track, and if you recall, there are just two wires running parallel to the tracks. That's the only thing that was still up, because this was the most sophisticated system that was used in our area, electronic jamming, special assets, combat assets, land/air battle, and all this was meant to sow panic and fear. What else can I say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Registrar, if we can go to Exhibit D1463, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall being promised that 200 men from the -- were you ever promised that 200 men from the Serbian SDB would be coming to Knin on the 5th?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, even if two brigades had -- were to come there, it would not be sufficient, let alone 200 men from the Serbian DB. I mean, maybe you can cheat little kids like that, you know, but that's -- that has nothing to do with reality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether it would have helped is another matter. Whether someone missed anything, the question simply was whether you recall that you were promised 200 Serbian SDB men would come to Knin, whether there was any such promise. Whether it realised is a different matter. That's simply the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question, please, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, do you recall both -- do you recall any conversation where Mr. Martic may have been on the phone with Mr. Stanisic and complained about Mr. Milosevic's behaviour?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't comment on that. I know that he was angry. He was angry with President Milosevic; Martic, I mean. But whom he was able to communicate with, I couldn't really ask him, because we didn't spend all the time together so that I could overhear his conversations. Whether someone had promised him those 200 men, I don't know. He didn't say anything to me, but to me this is just frivolous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, yesterday you mentioned to us the 11th Corps in Eastern Slavonia and that it never attacked out of Eastern Slavonia. And in the conversation on the screen, there is a statement: "M: Nothing without an ultimatum. Have those from the 11th left? I don't believe them -- anything. Did he stop them? "J: They will work tomorrow." M then says: "Have they worked today? To be honest, I don't believe anything. I believe he stopped them, too. He lied to me like the last time, too." Do you recall Mr. -- do you recall any conversation with Mr. Martic complaining that someone stopped the 11th Corps from attacking out of Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not out, but in Eastern Slavonia. I have to explain the essence. When I was receiving my assignment in Karadjordjevo, that is the substance, I was told this corps should be given to the corps commander and to Mrgud. They will work to prepare the forces and the people for cohabitation, and, you take these 4 Corps and do the same thing there. That corps will not be engaged, and that is why you were free to pull in your forces. That is a question to be put to Franjo and to Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We can't put those questions to them, General. Let me, Mr. President, say that in terms of -- if we look at this, and I'm doing this because we're at a break, Mr. President, to give everyone an opportunity. In this conversation, if we turn the page in English - stop right there - right in the middle of the page there's a reference that says: "MRK: No one expected that they would attack the town. I didn't attack Zagreb. Bastards. That's why I will strike it tomorrow."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you anything, so don't say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you'd say that -- let me just --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I promise you, Mr. President, that I would alert you to any issues before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, thank you for that. I'm just -- if we want to think it over, over the break, we have no access to our e-court system when we're not in this courtroom, when we're locked in here, so I'm just trying to find exactly what we are looking at. Apparently this is a --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is an intercepted conversation, Mr. President, which has been admitted into evidence and which the Defence asserts is a conversation at 2310 involving Mr. Martic, Mr. Mrksic, and Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this is -- let me just have a look. The exhibit number was one out of a series --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is D1463.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And I will also, after the break just -- as a general matter, I will address with him -- with this exhibit and Exhibit D930, which is Mr. Vrcelj's book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Specific pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe the English page is page 9; it begins at page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And D1463 is how long? It seems to be a whole series -- oh, it's only two pages. If there would be a possibility for me to have a print-out during the break, then I can read it, because I have no access to my electronic system. So I'm just asking the Registrar to provide me with hard copies of it. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you hoped that you would be able to finish today. Do you think you'll be able to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to push as hard as I can to get done by 1.45, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, let me now show you Exhibit D930; English page 10, B/C/S page 9. General, I'm going to show you an excerpt from a book written by Marko Vrcelj. Do you recall who Marko Vrcelj was?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... of artillery --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in the middle of page 9 in the B/C/S, and at the bottom of page 10 in the English - further down, please - it says: "In the afternoon, when the Orkan commander briefed me to have completed the tasks he has received, I ordered him to get ready to fire at the military targets ..." If we could turn the page in English, please: " ... in Zagreb and Dubo Selo, and that the fighting was to start at 0700 hours the following morning." And then if we go down to the third paragraph -- I'm sorry, if we could turn the page in English, please. If we could turn the page in English, please. Okay. It says -- sorry, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we have a lot of mistakes. You started saying it was page 10 in the English, then you read from the bottom of page 9. You asked to move to page 10, and now I think when this was about to be done, that it was then assumed we had to go to the next page anyhow. So I think we should be on page 10 of the English at the top now. Is that correct, Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at page 11 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at the paging at the bottom of the -- what you started reading appears on the bottom of page 9 in the paging of the document itself. And if we could go back one page, I think we are where we should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking for page 11 in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it true that you started reading what we see now in the bottom: "In the afternoon, when the Orkan command ..." and then you asked to move to the next page, which is -- there we are. I think we're now on the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "We headed up towards Srb at around 3.00 in the morning." And then it continues on: "Looking at the column of people leaving their homes to go to the unknown, knowing that the Orkan commander had gotten the task to fire at Zagreb, I had to reach the commander to tell him to tell the guy not to fire at Zagreb. If he was to fire any shells at Zagreb, the Ustashas would lift up their own air force and would mutilate these innocent people. That is the reason why I hurried up to find the commander before 6.00 so that we can prevent catastrophe in waiting." If we can scroll down in the B/C/S, please. And now, General Mrksic, I'd like to show you a video which is related to this issue of the shelling of Zagreb and the decision to shell Zagreb. And this is, I believe, a 12-minute video, Mr. President, and I will ask additional questions in addition to this topic based on that video. But transcripts have been provided the booths. We will stop it to allow the translation to catch up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Especially if someone would follow the translation, especially when it's not written. If there's no subtitles, for example, in French, we hardly ever find them, and that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, this is now a video of an interview with Mr. Martic taken in the fall of 1995, and this is D929. And, General, if you would just listen, and when it's done, I will pose a series of questions to you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "That first day, the 4th of August, you, yourself, were present when Knin was bombed along with other places. The Croats did not score any significant successes, other than shifts in the Dinara and Mali Alan in Velebit. Everything else somehow went according to its own course, and considering that Croats were in Zagreb that day, especially in shelters, expecting us to react by shelling them, we concluded there was no need to bomb Zagreb during those initial moments. What is quite indicative, though, is that I received five phone calls that day from Milan Babic from Milosevic's office for one sole purpose, which was to suggest that I do not bomb Zagreb. I took this information on record and responded that we would assess what to do in due course. No one from the authorities in Serbia, from the regime, contacted me. They simply bypassed me and all contacts were conducted with General Mrksic. Later on, I saw the same requests not to shell Zagreb. "In the evening at 7.30, the Croatian prime-time newsreel was on. We had a generator and electricity within the HQ, and the Croats announced the cessation of air raids -- air threats in Zagreb because a general of theirs, Tolj, I believe was his name, said that all citizens should go out of their shelters in Zagreb because the Serbs supposedly did not have the necessary range. I subsequently sent to General Mrksic the order to bomb Zagreb with all possible means at our disposal and with all the ammunition we had. He replied, Okay, I understand, as they say."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, we'll pause it right here, so let me ask you -- we'll continue with this video, but since this is the issue: Do you recall a conversation on the evening of the 4th with Mr. Martic in which he passed an order to you to bomb Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Martic, seeing what was happening to Knin, kept saying, Why would not we hit back, hit Zagreb? I couldn't accept it. I said, All right, and I told the chief of artillery to pull out the Orkan as soon as possible, to pull it out from firing positions and not to shell, because that would amount to retaliation. In my book, that would be cowardice, that would be the act of someone at a loss for a course of action and then just hit at random whatever you want. This was changed in the war plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, do you know why Mr. Vrcelj passed an order to shell Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Vrcelj did this as a sort of an automatic reaction. If you have no communications, you man your firing positions. And when I heard that that was being done, I called Vrcelj immediately and I told them to head for Dvor, to pull out towards Slasinje [phoen] and not to shell the Croatian positions. One of the reasons was because this is prohibited under the Geneva Conventions; namely, to shell civilian facilities, because those were civilian facilities. There were civilians there. I was being attacked by brigades from the Dinara. I was not being attacked by Zagreb or from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We'll play the rest of the video now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Unfortunately, nothing came of this order of mine; rather, to make things even more interesting, they replaced the commander of the Kordun Corps, Colonel Veljko Bosanac, behind my back for fear that I would directly issue him an order for such an attack, because they disposed of the assets up there. They replaced him and appointed a new guy so that the order couldn't possibly be executed, and unfortunately not a single shell fell onto Zagreb, even though we had millions of reasons to do so. And then the worst scenario took place, which was that at a given moment during my brief absence, an order that had been written a couple months prior in Belgrade was issued calling for action in accordance with orders to withdraw the army, which I wasn't even aware of."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is all in hindsight. This is in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "On that unfortunate day, the 4th of August, what was your last order as the supreme commander? "My last order was what I told you about the shelling of Zagreb at approximately 7.30 p.m., when I saw the Croats were broadcasting. But prior to that -- but prior to that, I had made a decision. Unfortunately, there was no one to consult with. This was at 5.00 p.m., to withdraw the civilian population from the cities which were under constant shelling, such as Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and the order clearly stated that the non-combat population was to withdraw to the villages which were not being shelled, ending with Srb and Lapac, which were in the Krajina and not in Sumadija. I passed such an order for one reason only, that was because I remembered Western Slavonia and the massive suffering of civilians there when I was attacked even by the Serbian regime, and all those who practiced different politics than my own, that this was a mistake. I said that I wouldn't repeat the same mistake and withdraw everyone, but that all those capable for military service along with myself were to take a rifle in their hands and fight for Krajina. Although later on numerous attempts were made to manipulate these facts, this was practically the key, that I passed the order for the army to withdraw, which later proved to be untrue. Because that same evening, I suggested to General Mrksic that we launch a counter-attack towards Dinara, that I personally lead the men, as I knew the Dinara area well, and that we could surprise the Croats, upon which he just stared at me blankly as if to say nothing would come of this."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, do you remember any discussion with Mr. Mrksic on the evening of the 4th about doing -- launching a counter-attack against Croatian forces on the Dinara?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is an interview that he gave to Banja Luka. You know how things work. After the fact, one should look for someone to blame. So I don't see why you're showing this video here at all. I don't see what purpose that serves. There is the decision made by the Supreme Defence Council, and that would be like to my -- sort of bewailing my own fate.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Now, I don't know about this famous order to withdraw the army; nor could I have even anticipated, considering that the Croats experienced no significant successes this far. I believed that the next day would be better for us, to our advantage, and it surely would have been. My absence from the headquarters, which lasted some two hours, was enough for General Mrksic to gather all of his corps commanders which he had appointed in the meantime with new men and to tell them to act in accordance with this new order which had been prepared by Milosevic some months before that. It was sufficient for me to have been absent for that period of time for this to be issued. My return to the headquarters, where I had gone previously in order to set up Radio Knin, for it to start functioning, as a false Radio Knin had been broadcast and was deceiving our people, so when I returned I was confronted with an odd situation. Everyone was whispering about something, those colonels, generals, and I couldn't hear what they were saying. But I believed these were minor issues having to do with command tactics and said to myself that this is okay, this was nothing serious. "Later in the evening, sometime around midnight, I went to get some rest because I hadn't slept for two days. However, I immediately received a phone call from Dr. Karadzic, Krajisnik. The lines were still functioning, and they needed to tell me something, to give me suggestions, so I couldn't sleep. It was then that Mile Mrksic suggested, regarding the command conditions, which were truly dire, that it was impossible to command from Knin, and it was time to go to Srb. And I said, That is out of the question. What Srb are you talking about? That is out of the question, under no circumstances. "After a certain period of time, after a half hour or so of whispering with some colonels, they suggested that we exit at Padjene, that there was a command post there, in the sense that a normal command was possible from there, and that such tactics would then be implemented, that the Croats would be deceived. I relented then and said, If you're going to Padjene, okay. They could barely wait. They simply collected their things. I didn't know that they had already dismantled everything at the headquarters, and they got up and left."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, General Mrksic, was there a decision to initially evacuate or move the command to Padjene on the evening of the 4th?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Padjene was a command post of the 7th Corps. It was on the way. It was the command post of the 7th Dalmatia Corps, and from there it was possible to direct fire both of Knin and the others that I already mentioned, so that we would stop the further advance of the Croatian forces. And the president went to that area, and he remained there for a while to rest. I couldn't wait for him to get up. I had to move on in order to set up the system and make sure that it's functioning at Srb. And as for Srb, the day before the command post was moved from -- had been moved from Srb already, beforehand, the previous day, and this is normal in tactical terms. I have no intention of commenting what the president was saying here about what happened next in Banja Luka. I don't want to comment on this. I think it's not fair.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I remained there with my men sometime -- until about 3.00 or 4.00 in the morning, and then I left for Padjene, where I found the following situation. First of all, I realised this was not a command post, as they had indicated to me. There was some form of communication system, but this is not what I expected. But I said to myself, okay, I guess they'll assemble it. They have good communications officers, and things will get better. I then asked to go and rest, and they immediately provided me with some sort of bed. My men, who had accompanied me, also rested a bit, and we awoke at around 8.00. There was shelling going on. However, this didn't bother me. It was Saturday, but it was odd that there was no -- there were no sounds. And then all of a sudden we jumped up and realised that there was no command located there. They simply abandoned the position without even having awakened me, which is truly shameful. "For some time on, we remained there around Padjene, and around 10.00, I went to search for the command, and only then did I realise, which I could not have possibly anticipated or even imagined that could happen, when I came across a unit which was in Zitnic, which I encountered at the end of Padjene, in Kravlja Draga as we call it, and these men told me that they had received orders to withdraw. What orders to withdraw? Get back there. The order to withdraw is invalid. I said I found their Commander Colonel Davidovic and asked him, what is this supposed to mean? The soldiers surrounded him, defended him, he is not to blame, he received an order. He was like a convict. "At the top of Otric, and I needed a few hours to break through, I encountered the brigade from Dinara. Now, you can only guess when I left, and it was there that I encountered our Colonel Radic. He was pulling his hair out, and he kept saying, Don't ask me anything, don't ask a thing, and so forth. I saw this was a strange situation. Where is Mrksic, I said. He replied, He was in Srb. Therefore, he had escaped to Srb. I needed a few hours as well from Srpski Klanac. I couldn't break through. I went to Srb on foot, only to find them in Srb, to find the famous headquarters which didn't even have a command, they didn't even have a telephone. I saw -- everything was nearly completely lost. I said, Mile, what is this supposed to mean? Do you have military police at your disposal? Stop these people, I will address them. I could -- he didn't even make any attempt. He said, well, you know, We'll do it in Petrovac."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, let me ask you, on the 5th of August when you were in Srb, were you already telling Mr. Martic that you would start arresting people once you get to Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I did not. All this is -- in fact, I'm not going to comment, who was supposed -- at whose door the blame was supposed to be laid? And I'm grateful that you called me to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to show you the rest of the video, because I want to finish today, so let me ask you this: He says in the video that you had told him on the 5th that you would start arresting people once you get to Petrovac. Was it your intention on the 5th to stay in Srb and to continue to mount a defence against HV forces?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know that on the 4th, in the evening, I assigned tasks to the 5th Infantry Brigade, so the Knin Corps would be deployed. And what should be done to prevent them from advancing from Gracac, and that the people should stay there -- a political solution. That very day, a helicopter was sent from Republika Srpska to Srb to get me and transfer me to Ostrelj, where Mladic told me, This is urgent, your people are perishing in Banija and Kordun. So I transferred to that theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But in terms of -- let's go back to D1511, Mr. Registrar. General, this is the order that we talked about yesterday. Now, you issued an order, in fact, on the 5th of August to continue to form a defence line; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to page 2 in the English, please, and this is the portion, General, that starts under the heading "Order." Now, in fact, again on the 5th you were trying to establish a new front-line against the advancing HV forces, correct, as you can see in paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, were you in Srb on the 6th?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Srb on the 6th, and then I also left Srb on that same day. I spent a night there at the new command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I went to Ostrelj by helicopter and straight on to Boskoski Novi -- Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in that paragraph 1, if you look at the order, I was referring earlier to you, I said -- I referred to a place called Bulina Strana, and in your order it says: "A part of the forces is to continue the battle in the encirclement, one unit is to be sent to the area of Bulina Strana for a defence of the area of Knin." Does that refresh your memory at all as to what Bulina Strana is?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is probably a feature above Knin, above the winding road that leads from Knin, the hairpin-curves road. I cannot speculate, because I do not have a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When you left Srb on the 6th, was it your intention to continue to resist Croatian Army forces that were advancing towards Srb?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intention was for us to stay there, to hold out and offer a resistance pending developments, and we were expecting something to be done by the international community. We were anticipating -- we were hoping that the international community would not allow people to be driven out of Krajina to Bosnia and to the Republika Srpska. We were expecting changes along those lines, so that is why I was frightened by what was happening in Banija and in Kordun, and that is why I sent word that the helicopters should find and get me -- should come and get me and take me to that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, General, why didn't you, on the 6th of August, surrender or offer -- or seek terms of surrender to the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why should I, when I was offering peace without war, a peaceful solution? And this did not suit you, the Croatian Army, the Croatian police. We had signed everything, the Z-4 in Geneva, and I was supposed to go and meet with Cervenko. I had all the necessary authority to sign a peaceful solution with him. Who was to go, was to go; the rest should remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, you're aware --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't need war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, you're aware that Cedo Bulat under in Sector North surrendered to General Stipetic of the Croatian Army; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And as a result of his surrender -- as a result of his surrender to the Croatian Army, he was allowed to leave his encirclements with his equipment and everything; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just for the men to leave without equipment, and officers were allowed to just carry their pistols. That is under the Geneva Convention. They had to surrender everything else, all the resources.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot follow the witness and did not catch the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, they didn't catch your last sentence, so if you could repeat just your last sentence. Just repeat what you said.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kordun Corps surrendered because it was cut off by air raids, and the line was cut off when Glina was taken, so the retreat line was cut off and the corps was forced to do fight in encirclement. Because that would entail great casualties among the civilians, the command of that corps decided to surrender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were invited to repeat your last sentence. Apparently, you have given us more information. Wait for the next question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what my last sentence was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic will put his next question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now my question to you is: Why -- you've now said what the Kordun Corps did. Because they were encircled and because great casualties would have occurred among civilians, the commander of the corps decided to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My question to you is: Why, on the entire territory -- you were the commander for the entire territory of the Krajina. Why didn't you, when you -- at the point you realised you could no longer defend, surrender, as Cedo Bulat did, in order to avoid, as to use your terms, great casualties?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the other corps were not yet in a position of having to surrender. A soldier can surrender when there is no-way-out position, and Cedo was in a no-way-out position. But Mr. Tudjman had sent a man who personally knew Cedo Bulat, and he had given him guarantees, so that they had established a relationship of trust, and there were guarantees being given that nothing would happen to the people if the corps pulled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So the only way you would have surrendered is if you were completely encircled; is that how I'm to understand you? Only if you're encircled would you ever surrender?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. That is what you wouldn't allow me to expound on when I said what changes were that I had undertaken. If a corps should be encircled, then each corps takes a decision in terms of what is the best for the people. And we reckoned that all the corps would fare like the Kordun Corps did, but that there would be no retaliation against the people. But you didn't just cut off; you pushed, you instilled fear in the people, you frightened the people, and people had to flee. You pushed and you pushed and you pushed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you have more than answered the question that was put to you. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, afterwards, after Operation Storm, you came under some criticism; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was to blame for everything to this day. And I would like to say how I fared. I'll be brief. I could not go back to Serbia. My entry was barred. I was threatened with arrest. I entered two months later by getting across the Drina, and then I was put under house arrest for two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, General, General --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter correction: I was put under house arrest and then I had to retire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm racing to try to finish -- we're done today. General -- if I could have 65 ter 1D1043, please. And let me show you a series of documents, and that will speed it up so we can finish today, Mr. President. I won't ask you to comment on each document. I'll ask you to comment on all of them when we've shown every document.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I've forgotten about these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm interested -- this purports to be a report or a communication from you to the chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army on the 18th of August. Point 6 says: "Organise --" you're conveying the decision of the Presidency, point 1. And then point 6 is: "Organise a group visit of military conscripts at refugee centres, with the aim of making lists and gathering volunteers. "The dead-line for implementation is 1 September 1995 until when a report is to be submitted." Number 12, it says - I think there's a mis-translation here, General, but: "At this moment, a volunteer battalion of the VRS has been a formed from Western Slavonians which, with the other volunteers, constitutes a core of units located on Mount Kozara in the settlement Benkovac. Upon formation, training, and preparation, the volunteers shall take over part of the battle-field on the RSK border, and in that manner assist the defence of the VRS." Mr. President, just for speed, if I could tender this now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1522.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have Exhibit 65 ter 1D1046, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a document purporting to be a communication from you, again, to the chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's see what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It looks like you're seeking, it says: "We seek that in the aim of enabling us to resolve the problems within the authority of the General Staff of the Serb Krajina Army, you provide the following assistance ..." And in point 4: "The General Staff and the SVK units' commands are located in the RS, where they are primarily working on training the units and their inclusion in the composition of the VRS." Mr. President, I ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D1523.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have Exhibit D416, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a directive from Mr. Martic on the 2nd of August -- 2nd of September -- or 4th of September, I'm sorry, where he is issuing a directive on the formation of the RSK Liberation Army, and its coalescing into the combat operations in the territory of the Republika Srpska and the RSK. And then let me flip to 65 ter 1D1047, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you'd like to tender the previous one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is already in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Martic issues that order on the 4th, and then there is a stamp in the original here, in the upper left-hand corner. This purports to be an order by you. The stamp is "7 September 1995," for the formation of the Liberation Army of the Republic of Serb Krajina, and its coalescing into combat operations in the territory of the RS and the RSK. And if we look at paragraph 2 of this order, it says: "The RSK Liberation Army is organised in liberation brigade, volunteer liberation brigades, and special units. "Special units are organised in groups and squads." Now, General Mrksic, do you recall issuing an order for the formation of the liberation Army of the RSK in September of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have nothing to say about this material, this document. We were – we were losers, and we wanted to reorganise and go back to our areas. We didn't go from there on purpose, to escape - we were pushed out, and we wanted to go back. And we were even prepared to switch to sabotage and terrorist, I mean anti-sabotage actions, reconnaissance and so on. That’s, I mean - you know how it is… It's like a government in exile, then you ask around, Can we, can we not? And we didn't even know that we were not allowed to mobilise refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, the simple question was whether you had any recollection in giving such an order. The answer apparently is "yes."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, in case there's an interpretation issue, what types of units did you say? You said: "We were even prepared to switch to ..."?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reconnaissance units that would go and gather data or information on the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. That was our territory. Of course, in coordination with the forces of Republika Srpska, because an offensive was being prepared against Republika Srpska, against Prijedor, Banja Luka, and so on. However, this was just a wish list, a laundry list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, General: Are you familiar with whether there were camps organised for bringing back from Serbia males from the Krajina so that they would be retrained and deployed in units such as these?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was one in Bijeljina and another one near Banja Luka, at - let me try to remember - the training-grounds at Manjaca. But people did not wish to take up arms, so this fell through. And this was also not within our powers, because no one had the right to force anyone to take up arms if they had already decided to give up fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was there a camp in Eastern Slavonia that you know of?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no prerogatives in Eastern Slavonia. I could not get involved, nor would they let me enter Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D1524, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, thank you very much. That completes my examination --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for inviting me to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we'll adjourn for the day, and we'd like to see you back on Monday at 9.00. And I'm quite confident that we'll be able to conclude your testimony in time. Mr. Misetic strictly kept to his time assessment, and I expect the other parties to do the same, which would not in any way endanger your personal interest next week. Could -- Mr. Mrksic, I would like again to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about the substance. You know the difference about the weather, fine; about your health, fine. But not about your testimony. Could Mr. Mrksic be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd like to deliver a very short decision, so that's from the table as well, and that is a decision on the admission of P2539. On the 9th of June, 2009, the Prosecution tendered P2539, of which it had put an excerpt to Witness Zuzul. The excerpt is from a news article according to which the witness had, on the 24th of July, 1997, and in his capacity as Croatian ambassador to the US, announced Croatia's resistance to orders by this Tribunal to produce documents implicating President Tudjman in the Bosnian war. The witness commented in court on the excerpt. All of this can be found between transcript pages 18374 and 18380. The Chamber admits P2539 into evidence because it provides the context to the witness's comments on the article, which may be difficult to understand and to evaluate in the absence of P2539. The Chamber is mindful that it is a hearsay statement. The Chamber further emphasizes that the admission is no indication of the weight, if any, which the Chamber may ultimately attach to this article. And this concludes the Chamber's decision on the admission of P2539. We adjourn, and we'll resume on Monday, the 22nd of June, 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 22nd day of June, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.51 p.m.,
